title: China's Economic Peak Is Behind It: Credit Stalls, Deflation Ahead
dek: China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has fallen since; credit growth has dropped from 18% to 5%, real growth may be just 1.5%-2%, and the US has outperformed for five straight years. The supply-chain-dominance narrative is falsified by the data; the future looks more like Japanese-style deflation.
why: It rebuts the mainstream narrative that China's new industries are a growth engine, grounding the call in credit, special bonds and demographic data — for anyone who wants to update their long-run view of the US and China.
who: Investors and researchers making macro calls on the US and China, and corporate decision-makers who treat China as a market or a supply-chain source; especially suited to anyone who wants to test the ‘China's new industries = growth engine’ narrative.
skip: The first 3 minutes of guest introduction and article preamble can be skipped; start at 1:16 with the data comparison.

points.h: China has already missed its window to overtake the US
points.body: Dmitri sets the frame with official data: China's share of global GDP peaked at 18.5% in 2021 and has declined every year since, while the US rose from 24% to about 26%. From this he concludes that not only is it nearly impossible for China to replace the US as the world's largest economy, but America's economic advantage may keep widening over the next decade. Logan agrees completely and steers the discussion toward a framework of ‘decay, not collapse.’

points.h: The root of China's slowdown is that credit expansion is over
points.body: Logan attributes China's slowdown to the end of extraordinary credit expansion. After the financial crisis China added credit equal to one-third of global GDP in eight years; credit growth averaged 18% from 2007-2016, fell to 9% after 2017, and is now slightly above 5%. Once credit stops, borrowers can no longer refinance and investment decelerates. Officials still report 5.2% growth for 2023 and 5% for 2024 and 2025, but he estimates real growth since 2022 at only 1.5%-2%, already below the US.

points.h: Scoring by purchasing power parity is rewarding deflation
points.body: To the common rebuttal that China has already overtaken the US on purchasing power parity, Logan says PPP comparisons still make sense for developing countries but do not hold between the world's two largest economies: scoring by PPP amounts to rewarding China for manufacturing deflation — the lower domestic prices are, the stronger the economy looks, and deflation is precisely the problem. He also stresses that debt is repaid in nominal local currency, so nominal GDP is what matters; and the exchange rate is not an exogenous variable but an external signal of China's policy capacity.

points.h: Capital controls are not a cure, they only buy time
points.body: Logan concedes that China's capital controls do work, but argues they are no panacea for a giant macro imbalance. The impossible trinity dictates that free capital flows, a stable exchange rate and independent monetary policy can be achieved at most two at a time. The function of capital controls is to slow outflows, suppress rapid cross-border volatility and channel outflows into channels the government can see — that Huawei and BYD can expand abroad on a large scale while the overseas M&A of private firms like HNA in 2016 was halted are two sides of this screening mechanism.

points.h: Credit is still subsidising old industries, not shifting to new ones
points.body: Logan rebuts the claim that credit is shifting toward higher-productivity new industries: central bank data show the share of loans issued at or below the Loan Prime Rate has risen from the low 20s% to 59%, meaning banks are continuously subsidising. The share of special revenue bonds going to so-called strategic industries rose only from about 2% to 6% between 2021 and 2025, with the vast majority still flowing to traditional sectors. Using the 2023 input-output tables, EVs, batteries, AI and solar together are about 6.3% of GDP, while the decline in property and infrastructure investment is roughly six times the increment from these new industries.

points.h: Europe is the last buyer of China's excess capacity
points.body: Logan judges that if Europe turns protectionist, China is ‘really finished’: the US market has already narrowed with limited room for transshipment, and the developing world cannot absorb China's excess capacity while sustaining its own growth. He warns that America's focus on the bilateral deficit is wrong — the deficit is determined by the savings-investment gap, and tariffs only redistribute it; failing to address the underlying imbalance will merely spawn more transshipment trade.

points.h: Without tax reform, domestic demand cannot get up
points.body: Logan compares the present to the Kosygin reform in the Soviet Union: Brezhnev chose the scientific-technological revolution over pushing reform and preserving ideology. For China to convert savings into consumption, the real lever is tax policy — extracting resources from high-net-worth individuals, state-owned enterprises and private firms shut out of the financial system. But he thinks it nearly unimaginable that Xi Jinping would go on television and declare that ‘the fiscal and financial system of the past 15 years no longer applies’; Beijing sticks to the 5% growth narrative partly to undermine export controls and deter Western investment in alternative supply chains.

points.h: China in 2035 will look like Japan today
points.body: Logan predicts that absent a dramatic policy shift, China's economy in 2035 will look more like Japan's: persistent deflation, persistent external surpluses, downward pressure on the exchange rate and low interest rates. The hardest constraint is demography — China's actual average age at death is 73, and the baby boom at the founding of the PRC will bring a population decline of 50-60 million over the next decade, about 3%-4% of the total; even holding the birth rate at last year's low of 7.92 million will not stop it. He also notes the fiscal deficit is already close to $2 trillion a year, 9.5% of GDP, leaving far fewer resources to draw on than in the past. Finally he says that if China really did win on export share, it would only provoke a stronger political backlash — ‘winning is losing.’

quotes.text: According to China's own economic data, which is chronically underreported, China peaked as a proportion of the global economy in 2021 at 18.5% of global GDP and has declined ever since.
China saw basically an expansion of around a third of global GDP in new credit in just eight years. And we've never seen anything like this.
China's financial system is a bunch of assets without markets for them.
it's not crisis or collapse, it's decay that you're seeing in terms of this pressure.
It doesn't have to be called a quote unquote financial crisis, but it has all the same consequences of a financial crisis.
The average age at which people die is 73 in China. And so there was a baby boom basically right after the end of the Civil War.
